messages.body_plain:
Vaughn

Specifically, the error you are encountering is caused by misconstruction of the dataframe region.table.  You have manufactured that dataframe of a single value of the region area of 155.5; hence the complaint about incorrect number of dimensions.  Help for dht describes this specification for region.table

region.table data.frame of region records. Two columns: Region.Label and Area.

Alternatively, you might investigate the R package Distance that is meant to be a simpler interface to the intricacies of the mrds package.  You should be able to use the flatfile data format, that would let you dispense with the sample.table, region.table and obs.table constructs.

Hello
I have a very general question on the use of the Distance program,
I am collecting vantage point samples of sea turtles around a small island, and would like to use Distance to estimate the density of turtles in different benthic habitats around the island. My concern is that although my survey method could be considered a point count  I am not actually viewing a circular sample area, as the turtles are only going to occur in the ocean part of my view not the land part. But i note that the calculations for determining probability density estimations and abundance in Distance include calculations that apply the radius of a circle from a point count. Does this matter? in the calculations for abundance could I simply measure the actual area covered by my vantage point count using Arcmap then input this area value in rather than  πw2  as the Distance manual suggests?.

Any thoughts/recommendations or suggested further reading would be much appreciated

Many thanks in advance
Louise

messages.body_plain:
Hi Louise,

I'm afraid it's not that simple!  The problem is your single point
sample is very far from the assumption in distance sampling that you
have a large number of samplers at random locations.  This assumption is
important because it means the true distribution of animal distances
with respect to your sampler locations is known -- for a point transect
the number of animals goes up linearly with distance from the point.
(If this is not a familiar concept to you, I'd recommend the free online
course at
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
particularly section 3).

One way round this is to assume the density of animals is uniform around
your vantage point, but this is almost never true -- animals certainly
will respond to the island (or at least change in depth) in some way or
another.  Luckily, you're not the first person to have this issue, and a
former PhD student here Martin Cox developed some methods that allow
estimation so long as detection probability is the same in every
direction and you have one covariate you can use to "explain" change in
animal density (e.g., depth).  There is an R package described in this paper

Cox, M., D.L. Borchers and N. Kelly.  2013. nupoint: An R package for
density estimation from point transects in the presence of nonuniform
animal density. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4: 589-594.
https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12058

and a nice application and explanation here:

Patricia Arranz, David L. Borchers, Natacha Aguilar Soto, Mark P.
Johnson and Martin J. Cox, A new method to study inshore whale cue
distribution from land‐based observations, Marine Mammal Science, 30, 2,
(810-818), (2013).
https://doi.org/10.1111/mms.12077

Hope this helps!

Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Louise,

Just one wee point to add to Len's helpful advice. If turtle distribution varies according to benthic habitat, and if benthic habitat variation is related to distance from your point, then you may struggle to disentangle the two. Imagine that the benthic stratum with the highest turtle densities is also the closest to your point. In such a situation, it is difficult (perhaps impossible, depending what other information is available to you) to distinguish between the effects of distance on detectability and the effects of habitat on actual density.

If this problem applies to your situation, the only solutions I can think of involve counting from situations where distance is not confounded with variables that could affect density. If there is another way around it, I'm sure Len and other Distance gurus on this forum can advise (and I will be eager to learn).

Best wishes,

Mark

Hello Everyone,

I would appreciate some reassurance about an approach I'm taking, using Distance in R. I can't find any other posts dealing with this (which makes me think I might be trying something odd, or something so simple it doesn't need asking about!)

Background
I have species counts from point transects in six different habitats. Species varied in their detectability, so I split them into three groups based on their maximum detection distance. Thus I have 18 Region.Labels (six habitats, each with three detectability groups). I had to bin the data as there was clear clumping at favoured distances.

I used MCDS with a Hazard Rate model, and habitat type and detectability group as covariates. Unfortunately, with the binned data, the chi-squared test for goodness-of-fit always gives p = 0. (I think this is because the chi-squared test is very sensitive to any discrepancy between observed and expected values? And my data do diverge). However, it is going to be the best I can do with this data. At least AIC favoured this model over all the others I tried.

Questions
I would now like to use the estimated probability of detection to modify the species counts according to habitat x detectability group. Although the summary(MODEL) gives "Average p", I am seeking probability at the covariate-level. I extracted these from the model summary (i.e. MODEL$ddf$fitted).

If I divide species count by the relevant fitted value, this should give number of individuals in the surveyed area for each habitat x detectability group(?)
e.g. 5 / 0.09288704 = 53.8

If I further divide this adjusted value by the surveyed area in hectares, I should get a count-per-hectare(?)
53.8 / 12.56637 = 4.3

These numbers seem reasonable to me. Does this seem right? Am I making any glaring errors?! I would really appreciate people's thoughts on my approach.

Many thanks,
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Tom

Lots packed into your message.  I'll set aside your goodness-of-fit challenge and speak to your abundance estimate method.

Generally speaking, you are using a Horvitz-Thompson-line estimator (where the detection probability is estimated).  This is described in Section 6.4 of Buckland et al. (2015).  The issues are

where to locate the necessary $\hat{P}$,
how to carry the uncertainty in the p-hat into the density estimate,
and are the derived species-specific estimates appropriate?
Item 1: You are correct looking at MODEL$ddf$fitted gives you detection probabilities in light of covariates.  But you'll need to take some care  to pair the proper fitted value matches your covariate levels.  They will appear in the object in the order the covariate levels are encountered in the data.

Item 2: You'll need a measure of precision to accompany those density estimates.  Application of the delta method will be needed.

Item 3: This is the least pleasant.  You are estimating detection probability at the "detectability group" level, but trying to estimate density at a lower level of aggregation (the species level).  In this situation, pooling robustness does not operate in your favour, and you may produce biased species-specific density estimates because you are using an incorrect estimated detection probability for each species.  As Buckland et al. (2015, Section 5.5.1) states

"If analyses are stratified, but a common detection is assumed for the separate strata, then stratum-specific abundance estimates are not pooling robust, although an estimate of overall abundances obtained by summing the stratum-specific estimates is."

Providing group-specific density estimates would put you on firmer ground.

Tom

Given you are attacking your data with covariates, why not have "species" as a covariate, rather than species-group?  Would the number of species, multiplied by the number of habitats, break the bank in terms of estimated parameters?

Delta method calculations are not readily available in Distance for the type of estimates you desire.  There are several packages in R that have delta method functions (alr3, modmarg), but I've not used them.  The method is discussed in this 2007 Condor paper by Larkin  https://doi.org/10.1650/0010-5422(2007)109[949:AVODPU]2.0.CO;2 <https://doi.org/10.1650/0010-5422(2007)109%5B949:AVODPU%5D2.0.CO;2>  If you produce group-specific density estimates, Distance will handle the uncertainty calculations for you.

However, I'm not sure how you will use your uncertainty measures in the diversity metrics you say you wish to compute.  Maybe some biodiversity researchers can pitch in on the subject of species-specific density and uncertainty in diversity measures.

Yikes, 250 species.....

The good news is that using species as a covariate allows the "borrowing of strength" across species, such that the "60-80" detections per species is not required.  That is the distinction between a stratum and a covariate.  However, modelling a species effect with covariates necessitates estimation of one parameter per species.

You might consider experimenting perhaps with one of your habitat types and a subset of species to see what might come from using species as a covariate.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am analyzing data from an aerial cetacean survey using a Trial configuration. Normally in such analyses the PI assumption is preferred because responsive movement is not expected and PI models almost always have better fit and lower AIC than the equivalent FI models. However I have one case where FI does fit well and has lower AIC than the PI model. It also produces a substantially (+40%) higher estimate than the PI model, which is also something I didn't expect, given the issue of possible unmodelled hetergeneity with FI models.

My question is: Is there any reason not to prefer an FI model in a case like this? I don't see any assumption violations so I am inclined to accept the FI model.

Thanks,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Hi ‘Distance’ users:

I have a question about how ‘Effort’ is incorporated into the abundance estimates produced by the ‘ds’ function, specifically, when using point transects.

I have been working with the Montrave robin point transect example. In this example, when a point is visited twice, effort =2. When the model is run, the summary of the results show that the ‘Covered area’ is equal to the number of points surveyed times the area of a point count circle times effort. So essentially, compared to one visit per site (effort=1), the area used to estimate density based on the abundance estimate (N.covered) is doubled when sites are visited twice.

This makes sense to me in that when a point is visited twice, we are surveying twice the area as when the point is visited once, thus the abundance estimate should apply to an area twice the size as if there was only one visit. However, fundamentally this does not make sense to me because we are surveying the same location (so the same area too), with the assumption that we are more or less going to detect the same individuals.

What is most confusing is that when we double the covered area for a point that is visited twice we dramatically reduce the density estimate.

Does the ds function somehow account for this? It seems to me that multiple visits should simply help reduce the variance associated with the abundance estimate, not increase the covered area, which in turn lowers the density estimate.

Thanks for any clarification on this!

Best,

Sam

messages.body_plain:
Sam, the clue is in the term ‘effort’.  If you visit each point twice, you double the effort and expect to double the number of detections.  It’s irrelevant that you may see the same birds on each visit – the 2 detection distances for the same bird are informative for estimating the detection function.  And if you do not double the covered area, you would find that density appears to double when you visit each point twice.

You do not ‘dramatically reduce’ the density estimate.  Expected density will not change, but precision will improve.  If you’re not finding that, then there is a problem with the code.

Steve Buckland

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of samuelg...@gmail.com
Sent: 18 January 2019 20:52
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] Confusion about the incorporation of Effort and Area for point transects

Hi ‘Distance’ users:

I have a question about how ‘Effort’ is incorporated into the abundance estimates produced by the ‘ds’ function, specifically, when using point transects.

I have been working with the Montrave robin point transect example. In this example, when a point is visited twice, effort =2. When the model is run, the summary of the results show that the ‘Covered area’ is equal to the number of points surveyed times the area of a point count circle times effort. So essentially, compared to one visit per site (effort=1), the area used to estimate density based on the abundance estimate (N.covered) is doubled when sites are visited twice.

This makes sense to me in that when a point is visited twice, we are surveying twice the area as when the point is visited once, thus the abundance estimate should apply to an area twice the size as if there was only one visit. However, fundamentally this does not make sense to me because we are surveying the same location (so the same area too), with the assumption that we are more or less going to detect the same individuals.

What is most confusing is that when we double the covered area for a point that is visited twice we dramatically reduce the density estimate.

Does the ds function somehow account for this? It seems to me that multiple visits should simply help reduce the variance associated with the abundance estimate, not increase the covered area, which in turn lowers the density estimate.

Thanks for any clarification on this!

Best,

Sam

messages.body_plain:
Jyoti

In the Distance for Windows software, a regression is performed roughly upon group size as a function of detection distance.  If the slope of the regression is significantly different from zero, this provides evidence that group size increases as a function of detection distance; implying small groups are not detected at large distances.  In this case, mean size of detected groups is a *biased* estimate of average group size in the population, and an adjusted estimate of expected group size should be used.

Watch and listen to the video/slides on this topic available in Chapter 5 of our online distance sampling workshop material for more details on this topic:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation

Tom

Yes Tom, similarity of the detection histograms is likely to be a better tool than maximum detection distance for species pooling.  Couple that with your biological knowledge of the species as well.  Good luck with this and let us know how you get on.

My interpretation is that if two species have similar histograms of detections, they are likely to share a detection function(?) In that case, rather than the crude pooling of species by maximum detection distance as I started out with, I could pool species with similar detection histograms. I can see this approach will be laborious in my case with 250 species, but would at least be consistent. First build a group of species with visually similar detection patterns, and then use AIC to contrast models with and without species as a covariate. If species covariate doesn't add anything to the model then I can assume the pooled group is legitimate.
>
> Even if I end up with 15 - 20 groups that would be much better than 250 individual species parameters-wise. I recognise this wouldn't work for species with low numbers of detections, (I would pool those in a "low-detections" group), but should be ok for those with sufficient detections to give the expected detectability curve. Does this sound ok?
>
> Kind regards,
> Tom
>
>

> >
> > Ewan
> >

In order to check the assumption that detectability is similar across species, I have compared models with and without species as a covariate. Based on AIC, the latter perform just as well as the former. This is helpful, because in my case degrees of freedom are very limited and much needed for other covariates which do have a large effect on the detection function. On Saturday, January 19, 2019 at 4:47:25 AM UTC-7, Stephen Buckland wrote:
>
> Sam, the clue is in the term ‘effort’.  If you visit each point twice, you double the effort and expect to double the number of detections.  It’s irrelevant that you may see the same birds on each visit – the 2 detection distances for the same bird are informative for estimating the detection function.  And if you do not double the covered area, you would find that density appears to double when you visit each point twice.
>
>
>
> You do not ‘dramatically reduce’ the density estimate.  Expected density will not change, but precision will improve.  If you’re not finding that, then there is a problem with the code.
>
>
>
> Steve Buckland

>

>
> Hi ‘Distance’ users:
>
>
>
> I have a question about how ‘Effort’ is incorporated into the abundance estimates produced by the ‘ds’ function, specifically, when using point transects.
>
>
>
> I have been working with the Montrave robin point transect example. In this example, when a point is visited twice, effort =2. When the model is run, the summary of the results show that the ‘Covered area’ is equal to the number of points surveyed times the area of a point count circle times effort. So essentially, compared to one visit per site (effort=1), the area used to estimate density based on the abundance estimate (N.covered) is doubled when sites are visited twice.
>
>
>
> This makes sense to me in that when a point is visited twice, we are surveying twice the area as when the point is visited once, thus the abundance estimate should apply to an area twice the size as if there was only one visit. However, fundamentally this does not make sense to me because we are surveying the same location (so the same area too), with the assumption that we are more or less going to detect the same individuals.
>
>
>
> What is most confusing is that when we double the covered area for a point that is visited twice we dramatically reduce the density estimate.
>
>
>
> Does the ds function somehow account for this? It seems to me that multiple visits should simply help reduce the variance associated with the abundance estimate, not increase the covered area, which in turn lowers the density estimate.
>
>
>
> Thanks for any clarification on this!
>
>
>
> Best,
>
> Sam
